review.notes: Built only on the course models (Lewin, force field, Kotter, power/interest grid, ADKAR barrier point, Kotter-Schlesinger, communication order, utilisation and proficiency formulas). Calculations checked. Fictional company.

content.company: Meridian Beverages (fictional), a drinks distributor with 140 sales reps and 3 depots
content.briefing: The board approved a new ordering app: every rep must take orders on a tablet instead of paper by the end of the quarter. The IT build is on time. You lead the people side. Go-live is in 10 weeks.

variants.text: The CEO calls it 'a small IT project'. 140 reps will change how they work every day, and paper ordering will be switched off. How do you size it?

choices.t: Transformational for the reps: many people, daily habits, hard to go back
choices.f: Correct. You get a sponsor, a plan and a budget for the people side, not just for IT.

choices.t: Incremental: the order process is the same, only the tool is new
choices.f: Every rep changes a daily habit and paper is removed. Treating big change as a small project is a classic mistake.

choices.t: Too early to say; size it after go-live, when real usage data exists
choices.f: Sizing decides how much structure you need. Waiting means discovering it at go-live.

variants.text: The IT manager says: 'The system works in testing, so the change is done.' What do you answer?

choices.t: The technical side is ready; the people side is whether reps adopt it
choices.f: Correct. A system that is installed but not used delivers nothing.

choices.t: Agreed; once training is booked, adoption will follow
choices.f: Training is one step. Desire, ability and reinforcement still decide adoption.

choices.t: Partly; we should first add more features reps asked for
choices.f: Listening to users helps, but it is still the technical side. The people plan is missing.

variants.text: Your force field analysis scores: driving forces 4 + 3 + 4 = 11. Restraining forces: fear of being tracked 5, slow 3G at depot B 4, habit 3 = 12. What is your first action?

choices.t: Reduce the strongest restraining forces: tracking fears and depot B signal
choices.f: Correct. The restraining side is stronger (12 against 11). Reducing the top restraining forces first shifts the balance.

choices.t: Add more driving forces, such as a bonus for early adopters
choices.f: It can help, but pushing harder against strong restraining forces raises resistance. Reduce them first.

choices.t: Go ahead; 11 and 12 are close enough to balance
choices.f: The restraining side is winning. Ignoring it means slow adoption and workarounds.

variants.text: You list the restraining forces from the head office. A depot supervisor says your list is wrong. What do you do?

choices.t: Run the analysis with reps and supervisors at each depot
choices.f: They add 'orders lost when the signal drops', which no one in the office knew. Diagnose with the people affected.

choices.t: Keep your list; supervisors often defend old habits
choices.f: Guessing restraining forces from the office is a common mistake. You miss the real blockers.

choices.t: Ask the supervisor to email any missing points
choices.f: Better than nothing, but one email gives one view. Workshops with the people affected find more.

variants.text: You form a guiding coalition. Who must be in it?

choices.t: The sponsor, depot heads, expert reps and respected supervisors
choices.f: Correct: position power, expertise, credibility and leadership, including people who could block it.

choices.t: The IT team and the project manager, to move fast
choices.f: No position power or credibility with reps. The coalition must include those who could block it.

choices.t: Only senior managers, so decisions are quick
choices.f: Power is there, but without expert users and trusted supervisors, the design and the message suffer.

variants.text: The sponsor signed the business case but has not appeared since. Reps say 'head office does not really care'.

choices.t: Ask the sponsor to open the depot briefings and visit each depot
choices.f: Reps see the sponsor in person. 'No sponsor, no change': visible, not just a signature.

choices.t: Send a strong email in the sponsor's name
choices.f: An email helps a little, but reps judge commitment by presence.

choices.t: Ignore it; the depot managers can carry the message
choices.f: Without a visible sponsor, depot managers lack backing when resistance comes.

variants.text: Draft vision: 'Project ORBIT phase 2: digital order capture enablement.' What do you do with it?

choices.t: Rewrite it in plain words with benefits reps care about
choices.f: New version: 'Orders in seconds, no lost paper, commission visible the same day.' People must understand and care.

choices.t: Keep it; a project name gives the change an identity
choices.f: A project name is not a vision. Reps cannot explain it, so they cannot buy into it.

choices.t: Add a long slide deck to explain what ORBIT means
choices.f: A vision that needs a deck fails Kotter's five-minute test. Make it short and concrete.

variants.text: Week 4. People ask for proof the app helps. What short-term win do you plan?

choices.t: Publish depot A's pilot: same-day commission statements for all reps
choices.f: Visible, clear and linked to the change. Reps at other depots start asking when they get it.

choices.t: Report that 92% of the IT test cases passed in the last test cycle
choices.f: Not visible or meaningful to reps. A win must matter to the people who change.

choices.t: Wait for full go-live results so the benefit shown is fully proven
choices.f: Real results take months. Plan wins along the way, do not hope for them.

variants.text: Power/interest grid: the national sales director has high power but low interest in the app. Where do you place him and how do you engage?

choices.t: Keep satisfied: short updates and consult him on decisions
choices.f: Correct. He stays supportive and approves the depot B signal budget when you ask.

choices.t: Monitor: he is not interested, so do nothing
choices.f: High power means he can stop the change. Ignoring him is a risk.

choices.t: Keep informed: send him the weekly newsletter
choices.f: Keep informed is for low-power, high-interest groups. He needs more direct attention.

variants.text: Supervisor Rosa: power 4, now Resistant (2), needs to be Leading (5). Supervisor Tomás: power 2, now Neutral (3), needs Supportive (4). Who comes first?

choices.t: Rosa: priority 4 x 3 = 12 against 2 x 1 = 2 for Tomás
choices.f: Correct: priority = power x gap. You meet Rosa one-to-one this week.

choices.t: Tomás: he is closer to supporting, so a quick win
choices.f: Easy is not important. Spend time where power and gap are highest.

choices.t: Both together in a group meeting
choices.f: Efficient, but Rosa's resistance needs a one-to-one conversation first.

variants.text: ADKAR scores for rep Paulo: Awareness 4, Desire 2, Knowledge 2, Ability 1, Reinforcement 1. What do you do first?

choices.t: Work on Desire: what is in it for him
choices.f: Correct. The barrier point is the first score of 3 or lower, which is Desire. More training would not fix it.

choices.t: Coach Ability, since it is his lowest score
choices.f: Fix the first barrier, not the lowest score. Without desire, he will not practise.

choices.t: Send him to the next training session
choices.f: Answering low Desire with more training is a common mistake.

variants.text: ADKAR scores for rep Ana: Awareness 5, Desire 4, Knowledge 3, Ability 2, Reinforcement 1. What do you do first?

choices.t: Train her: Knowledge is the first score of 3 or lower
choices.f: Correct. After training, you check Ability with practice.

choices.t: Recognise her publicly to boost Reinforcement
choices.f: Reinforcement comes last. Fix the first barrier first.

choices.t: Pair her with a champion for practice
choices.f: Practice builds Ability, but she first needs to know how. Train, then practise.

variants.text: Depot B reps resist: they believe the tablet will be used to track and punish them. Which approach first?

choices.t: Education and participation: show what is tracked and involve them in the rules
choices.f: Correct. Misunderstanding and low trust call for the first three approaches. Reps help write the data-use rules.

choices.t: Tell them clearly that tablet use is mandatory from Monday onwards
choices.f: Coercion first turns misunderstanding into hostility.

choices.t: Offer depot B a cash bonus for every week the tablets are used
choices.f: Negotiation can work, but it does not fix the misunderstanding. Explain first.

variants.text: A rumour spreads on WhatsApp: 'the app will replace 20 reps'. It is false. What do you do?

choices.t: Have supervisors answer it face to face this week, with facts
choices.f: Correct. Rumours are answered fast, face to face, through the line.

choices.t: Send a company-wide email next month with the facts
choices.f: Too slow and too distant. The rumour grows for a month.

choices.t: Ignore it; responding gives it attention
choices.f: Ignoring rumours is a listed mistake. Silence looks like confirmation.

variants.text: The launch announcement is ready. In which order do people hear it?

choices.t: Sponsor and coalition, then supervisors, then team briefings
choices.f: Correct. Supervisors are briefed first, with a script and a question list, so they can answer their teams.

choices.t: Everyone at once by email, so it is fair
choices.f: Teams then ask supervisors questions they cannot answer. Trust travels through the line.

choices.t: Reps first, then supervisors, so reps hear it directly
choices.f: Teams hearing news before supervisors is a listed mistake.

variants.text: Who should explain 'what changes for me' to the reps?

choices.t: Their direct supervisor
choices.f: Correct. Senior leaders give the business reasons; direct supervisors explain what it means for each person.

choices.t: The CEO, in a recorded video
choices.f: Good for the business reasons, but reps want 'what it means for me' from the person they report to.

choices.t: The IT vendor's trainer
choices.f: Wrong sender. The vendor knows the system, not the reps' day.

variants.text: Four weeks after go-live: 140 target reps, 98 placed at least one order on the tablet this week. What is utilisation?

choices.f: Correct: 98 / 140 x 100. Next you ask: who are the 42, and why?
That is the number of reps, not the percentage. Utilisation = active users / target users x 100.

choices.t: Cannot tell without counting logins
choices.f: Count real use, not logins. Orders placed is the right measure.

variants.text: This week: 2,400 orders on tablets, 2,160 with no error. What is proficiency?

choices.f: Correct: 2,160 / 2,400 x 100. Using it is not the same as using it well.
That is the error rate. Proficiency = error-free / total x 100.

choices.t: It is the same as utilisation
choices.f: Utilisation measures use; proficiency measures quality of use.

variants.text: Month 3: some reps are back on paper because old order books are still in the depots. What do you do?

choices.t: Remove the old order books and make managers ask about tablet orders
choices.f: Correct. Remove the way back and keep managers asking. Use returns to target.

choices.t: Accept paper from reps who prefer it, as long as targets are met
choices.f: The change slides back. Old forms still available is a top reason for failure.

choices.t: Send a firm reminder email to all reps about the tablet rule
choices.f: A reminder helps briefly, but while paper exists, the old way stays easy.

variants.text: Utilisation reached 95%. The project budget ends this month. What do you do?

choices.t: Hand over to a named business owner with measures and a review meeting
choices.f: Correct. Close the project, not the change. The owner keeps the measures alive.

choices.t: Close the project and celebrate with the team; the target is met
choices.f: Celebrate, yes, but without an owner and measures, the change can still slide back.

choices.t: Keep the project team in place for another year, just to be safe
choices.f: That avoids handover. The business must own the change, not the project team.
